name: Тура позаду пішака
description:
Chess is full of wisdom. One piece of wisdom is that a rook must stand behind the passed pawn. This applies to both the attacker and the defender. The idea behind this is as follows:

  • The rook defends the pawn when the pawn moves forward.
  • If the rook is behind the other player's passed pawn, then the pawn cannot advance (unless it is defended along the way).

Pictures often provide more clarity than words, so let's look at the examples.

In Example 1, we see that placing the rook behind one's own passed pawn gives White the win.

In example 2, black places the rook behind the other player's passed pawn and thus makes a draw.

In Example 3, black can do the same as in Example 2, but it is awkward. The attacker then also places the rook behind the passed pawn and wins. It is better to give an intermediate check and then place the rook behind the other player's passed pawn. Black then wins the pawn.

In Example 4, as in Examples 2 and 3, a black rook is behind the passed pawn. This time black does not win the pawn, but because the white rook stands in front of its own pawn, the pawn does not advance either. The position is a draw.

What do you have to do?

Place the rook (cleverly) behind the passed pawn and cash in on your advantage.

Are you defending? Then place the rook (cleverly) behind the other player's passed pawn and make a draw.

examples.text: 1.Ra1. White places the rook behind the passed pawn. 1...Ra8. Black stops the pawn, but this means that the rook can no longer move without letting White promote. Notice the difference in freedom between the rooks. The further forward the pawn is moved, the larger the space for the rook behind the passed pawn and the smaller the space for the rook in front of the passed pawn. Now that the black rook can't do anything, it's time to bring in the king! 2.Kc5 Kd7 3.Kb6 Kc8. Black is just in time to prevent white from attacking the black rook. It is good to reflect on this position for a moment. What should black do next move? The rook cannot really move and if the king moves, the white king is going to attack the rook via b7. In short, black on the move is in zugzwang. A waiting move (remember that clever trick we used when mating with the rook?) is now sufficient: 4.Ra2 Kd7 5.Kb7.
With 1...Ra6 Black places the rook behind the other player's passed pawn. White can no longer defend the pawn.

Logical here seems 1...Ra6, but after 2.Ra2 white can place a rook behind the passed pawn. The pawn then walks through or black has to give their rook for the pawn.

Better is to give an intermediate check first: 1...Rb6+!. If the king moves to the a-line, black plays 2...Ra6+ (check!) and white has no time to play the rook to a2. After 2.Kc3 black also plays 2...Ra6 and white can no longer defend the pawn. The game will end in a draw.

As in Example 1, here we see a big difference in freedin between the rook behind and in front of the passed pawn. In this case, it is the defender who has the rook behind the passed pawn.

What is important here is that the passed pawn is covered in two ways. If white is to move, they can remove the rook and promotion can only be prevented by giving the rook in front of the pawn. With rook and king against king, by now you know how to mate!

Black to move doesn't let this happen, of course: 1...Rb1+. Black tries to dislodge the white king from the pawn. If white sticks to the pawn, they won't get any further: 2.Ka6 Ra1+ 3.Kb6 Rb1+. If white releases the pawn, then the rook returns to the a-line, because otherwise white has time to remove their rook: 4.Kc5 Ra1. If white now moves the rook, then black can capture the pawn. When white puts the king on b6, black gives another check on the b-file and then returns to the a-file. If white does something else with the king, then black can wait patiently by playing the rook back and forth between a1 and a2, for example. The rook stays behind the passed pawn. White cannot make progress. It will be a draw!

texts: Rooks belong behind passed pawns, even those of the opponent.
